draft.title: Areas needing action
card: Health data counts how many young people have a health problem, are hurt by it or die from it. Researchers use it to see which problems affect the most young people.
Data can also show which problems are growing, which groups are hit hardest and which cause the most harm. These problems are the ones that most need action.
In Australia, areas often named for young people include mental health, injury and alcohol use. Governments and health groups can change their priorities as the data changes.
Action is aimed at where the data shows the greatest need. A problem that affects few young people or is falling is less of a priority.
draft.remember: Health data shows where young people most need action, so priorities are chosen from evidence.

a.q: Why does a health agency use data to choose areas of youth health to act on?
opts: It shows which problems affect and harm many young people
It shows which problems young people find most interesting
It shows which problems are cheapest for the agency to fix
It shows which problems adults have stopped worrying about
a.why: Data counts how many young people are affected and how badly, so it points to the greatest need. Cost and interest are not what the data measures, so they do not decide the priority.
a.clue: Think about what the numbers count.

b.q: A state report finds that hospital visits for injury among 15 to 19 year olds have risen for five years, while visits for another problem have fallen. What should the health department most likely do?
opts: Make injury a priority area for action
Make the falling problem the main priority
Wait, because rising numbers are not a concern
Ignore the data until a young person dies
b.why: Rising injury visits show a growing problem, so it needs action. The falling problem is less urgent, though the data does not mean it has gone. Waiting for a death ignores what the data already shows.
b.clue: Which problem is growing in the data?

a.best: It shows which problems affect and harm many young people

b.best: Make injury a priority area for action

problems.detail: "A problem that affects few young people or is falling is less of a priority" overgeneralises. A falling problem that still affects many young people, or a rare problem that causes severe harm such as death, can remain a priority. This also sits awkwardly with the card's earlier point about problems that cause the most harm.

The why says cost is not what the data measures and does not decide priority. Health data often includes costs, and cost and cost-effectiveness are real factors in setting priorities. Costs are also the subject of point 5. The why should not state that cost plays no part.

The distractors ('Wait, because rising numbers are not a concern', 'Ignore the data until a young person dies') are implausible. A Year 11 student could pick the answer without understanding the idea, which makes the question too easy.

proposal.title: Areas needing action
card: Health data counts how many young people have a health problem, are hurt by it or die from it. Researchers use it to see which problems affect the most young people.
Data can also show which problems are growing, which groups are hit hardest and which cause the most harm, such as death or lasting injury.
In Australia, areas often named for young people include mental health, injury and alcohol use. Governments and health groups can change their priorities as the data changes.
Action is aimed where the data shows the greatest need. No single measure decides this: how common, how fast-growing and how harmful a problem is are weighed together.
proposal.remember: Priorities come from evidence: how many young people a problem affects, how it is changing and how much harm it does.

a.q: Why does a health agency use data to choose areas of youth health to act on?
opts: It shows which problems affect and harm many young people
It shows which problems get the most attention in the media
It shows which problems young people find most interesting
It shows which problems adults say they worry about most
a.why: Data counts how many young people are affected and how badly, so it points to the greatest need. Media attention, interest and worry reflect what people talk about, not how many young people are actually harmed.
a.clue: Think about what the numbers count.

b.q: A report finds alcohol-related harm among young Victorians has fallen slightly, but it still affects far more of them than any other problem in the report. What does this mean for action?
opts: It can stay a priority, as it still harms many young people
It can be dropped, as a falling trend means it is solved
It should wait for action until the trend rises again
It ranks below any problem that is rising, however small
b.why: Priorities weigh how common, how fast-growing and how harmful a problem is together. A slight fall does not change the fact that this problem still harms more young people than any other. Dropping it confuses a falling trend with a solved problem.
b.clue: Does a small fall change how many are still affected?
